'''''Kunzea ambigua''''', commonly known as '''white kunzea'''<ref name="RBGV">{{cite web |last1=Jeanes |first1=Jeff |last2=Stajsic |first2=Val |title=''Kunzea ambigua'' |url=https://vicflora.rbg.vic.gov.au/flora/taxon/8ab1ceeb-e54b-47cc-b185-cdc058f95a03 |publisher=Royal Botanic Gardens Victoria |access-date=28 October 2025}}</ref> or '''tick bush''',<ref name="RBGS">{{cite web |last1=Wilson |first1=Peter G. |title=''Kunzea ambigua'' |url=https://plantnet.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/cgi-bin/NSWfl.pl?page=nswfl&lvl=sp&name=Kunzea~ambigua |publisher=Royal Botanic Garden, Sydney |access-date=28 October 2025}}</ref> is a species of flowering plant in the family [[Myrtaceae]] and [[endemic]] to eastern [[Australia]]. It is an erect shrub with linear to narrowly lance-shaped leaves and white, more or less [[Sessility (botany)|sessile]] flowers and [[Dehiscence (botany)|dehiscent]] fruit.

==Description==
''Kunzea ambigua'' is an erect shrub that typically grows to a height of {{cvt|2–4|m}} and has young stems covered with shaggy hairs. The leaves are arranged alternately, linear to narrowly lance-shaped, {{cvt|4–12|mm}} long and {{cvt|1.0–1.5|mm}} wide on a [[Petiole (botany)|petiole]] about {{cvt|0.5|mm}} long. The flowers are white, more or less sessile, crowded on leafy side branches or in the axils of upper leaves. The [[sepal]]s are narrowly triangular, {{cvt|1.5–2.0|mm}} long and the petals the same length, the [[stamen]]s {{cvt|3–5|mm}} long. The [[Ovary (botany)|ovary]] usually has three [[locule]]s and the [[Style (botany)|style]] is {{cvt|5|mm}} long. Flowering mainly occurs from October to January, and the fruit is dehiscent, {{cvt|2.5–3.5|mm}} long and {{cvt|3–4|mm}} in diameter.<ref name="RBGV" /><ref name="RBGS" />

==Taxonomy and naming==
''Kunzea ambigua'' was first formally described in 1797 by [[James Edward Smith (botanist)|James Edward Smith]] who gave it the name ''Leptospermum ambiguum'' in the ''[[Transactions of the Linnean Society of London]]''.<ref name=APNI(1)>{{cite web|title=''Leptospermum ambiguum''|url= https://id.biodiversity.org.au/instance/apni/496951|publisher=APNI|access-date=2 September 2017}}</ref><ref name="Sm.">{{cite journal |last1=Smith |first1=James Edward |title=Botanical Characters of Some Plants of the Natural Order of Myrti. |journal=Transactions of the Linnean Society of London |date=1797 |volume=3 |page=264 |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/12864797#page/324/mode/1up |access-date=28 October 2025}}</ref> In 1917, English botanist [[George Claridge Druce]] transferred the species to ''Kunzea''.<ref name=APNI>{{cite web|title=''Kunzea ambigua''|url= https://id.biodiversity.org.au/instance/apni/467374|publisher=APNI|access-date=2 September 2017}}</ref> The generic name honours German naturalist [[Gustav Kunze]],<ref name=EJ15>{{cite book |last1=Elliot |first1=Rodger W. |last2=Jones |first2=David L. |last3=Blake |first3=Trevor |title=Encyclopaedia of Australian Plants Suitable for Cultivation: Volume 6 (K-M)|year=1993|page=15 |publisher=Lothian Press |location=Port Melbourne |isbn=0-85091-589-9}}</ref> while the [[Botanical name|specific epithet]] is derived from the [[Latin]] adjective ''ambiguus'' meaning "doubtful" or "uncertain".<ref>{{cite book|author = Simpson DP| title = Cassell's Latin Dictionary  | publisher = Cassell Ltd.| date = 1979|edition = 5|location = London|pages = 883| isbn=0-304-52257-0}}</ref>

A pale pink-flowered hybrid with ''[[Kunzea capitata]]'' has been recorded from Stony Range Flora reserve in [[Dee Why, New South Wales|Dee Why]] in Sydney's northern beaches region.<ref name = "AP73">{{cite journal |last = Blombery| first = Alec |date=June 1973 | title = ''Kunzea ambigua'' | journal = Australian Plants | volume = 7 | issue = 55 | pages = 133}}</ref>

==Distribution and habitat==
''Kunzea ambigua'' is found from northeastern [[New South Wales]], having been recorded in the Grand High Tops of the [[Warrumbungle National Park]],<ref name = "Martin80">{{cite journal |last = Martin| first = Rhonda |date=September 1980 | title = The Warrumbungle National Park: The flora as you will see it | journal = Australian Plants | volume = 10 | issue = 84 | pages = 376–80}}</ref> through [[Victoria (Australia)|Victoria]] and into [[Tasmania]]. It grows on [[sand]]y soils in coastal or near-coastal regions. It is a very common dry forest shrub of the Sydney region, and regenerates in disturbed or cleared areas.<ref name="Sydney">{{cite book |last1=Fairley |first1=Alan |last2=Moore |first2=Philip |title=Native Plants of the Sydney District |date=1989 |publisher=Kangaroo Press |location=Kenthurst, N.S.W. |page=188}}</ref> It is associated with scrub she-oak (''[[Allocasuarina distyla]]''), ''[[Melaleuca nodosa]]'', cheese tree (''[[Glochidion ferdinandi]]'') in heath or scrub, and with red bloodwood (''[[Corymbia gummifera]]''), peppermint gum (''[[Eucalyptus piperita]]''), forest red gum (''[[Eucalyptus tereticornis]]''), woolybutt (''[[Eucalyptus longifolia|E. longifolia]]''), thin-leaved stringybark  (''[[Eucalyptus eugenioides|E. eugenioides]]''), and white feather honeymyrtle  (''[[Melaleuca decora]]'') in forested areas. In [[Wilsons Promontory]] in Victoria, ''Kunzea ambigua'' is the dominant species within scattered areas of treeless heath that occur on granite hills and mountains.<ref name=Sibley>{{cite report|author1=Sibley, G.T. |author2=Rees, D.B. | title = A classification of the lands at Wilson's Promontory - Second Edition  | publisher = Centre for Land Protection Research (Vic))| date = July 1999| isbn=0-7306-6778-2|url=http://www.greenhouse.vic.gov.au/DPI/Vro/wgregn.nsf/0d08cd6930912d1e4a2567d2002579cb/db7185f46dd514d1ca2574ef001a6eed/$FILE/Wilsons%20Prom%20Report.pdf|access-date=11 January 2012}}</ref>

==Ecology==
Insects are the main pollinators of ''Kunzea ambigua''; these include various types of beetles including jewel beetles ([[Buprestidae]]), scarab beetles ([[Scarabaeidae]]), flower beetles ([[Mordellidae]]), and checkered beetles ([[Cleridae]])<ref>Webb, G.A. (1986) Some insect pollinators of Kunzea ambigua (Sm.) Druce (Myrtaceae) near Sydney, New South Wales. Victorian Naturalist 103: 12–15.</ref> as well as butterflies, flies, bees and wasps.<ref name="Ben98">{{cite journal |last1=Benson |first1=Doug |last2=McDougall |first2=Lyn |title=Ecology of Sydney Plant Species |journal=Cunninghamia |date=1998 |volume=5 |issue=4 |page=938 |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/269917#page/164/mode/1up |access-date=28 October 2025}}</ref> Tick bush is killed by fire and regenerates from seed. Plants can also colonise unburnt sites with ample sunlight.<ref name=Ben98/>

==Use in horticulture==
It was one of the first species of Australian plant introduced into cultivation in England.<ref name=EJ15/> It is a hardy and adaptable plant that is used in windbreaks and [[sand dune stabilization]] plantings, as well as gardens, particularly in Australian gardens using native plants according to principles of [[natural landscaping]]. The species attracts Australian native insects,<ref>{{cite book |title=Attracting Wildlife to Your Garden |last=Elliot |first=Rodger |author-link=Rodger Elliot |year=1994 |publisher=Lothian Books |location=Melbourne |isbn=0-85091-628-3 |pages=51}}</ref> and can provide shelter for small birds and the [[long-nosed bandicoot]] (''Perameles nasuta'').<ref>{{cite book |title=Missing Jigsaw Pieces: The Bushplants of the Cooks River Valley|last=Benson |first=D |author2=Ondinea D |author3=Bear V  |year=1999 |publisher=Royal Botanic Gardens, Sydney |location=Sydney |isbn=0-7313-9128-4|pages=57 }}</ref>
